idempotency.title: The same payment, sent twice
idempotency.alt: A recorded run on PostgreSQL. Two sessions send the same payment with one idempotency key, as a retry would. The second insert waits for the first to commit, then inserts nothing, so the customer is charged once.

steps.note: A client sends a payment, with a key it generated.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO payments VALUES ('019a0000-0000-7000-8000-000000000001', 100) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
steps.note: The row is in, but not committed yet.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO payments VALUES ('019a0000-0000-7000-8000-000000000001', 100) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
steps.note: The client timed out and retried with the same key. The database can't tell yet whether the first try will commit, so it waits.
The first try commits. The retry's insert returns having inserted nothing.

follower-cost.title: The cost of one new follower
follower-cost.alt: Time to record one new follower as a user's follower count grows from a thousand to a million. Inserting a row into a follows table stays flat at under a millisecond. Appending to a JSON array on the profile row grows with the size of the list, because the whole row is rewritten.

race-postgres.title: Insert speed by primary key: Postgres
race-postgres.alt: Rows inserted per second into a Postgres table with three kinds of primary key, as the table grows to three million rows. Sequential integers and UUIDv7 keep their speed. Random UUIDv4 falls behind as the index outgrows memory.

race-mysql.title: Insert speed by primary key: InnoDB
race-mysql.alt: Rows inserted per second into an InnoDB table with three kinds of primary key, as the table grows to two million rows. Because the table is stored in primary key order, random keys fall far behind, while ordered keys hold their speed.

bloom-index.title: Postgres has a Bloom index too
bloom-index.hint: One signature per row, from any of the indexed columns. It answers equality on any combination of them, and false positives are rechecked against the table.
bloom-index.query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, SUMMARY OFF)
SELECT * FROM products WHERE size = 7 AND brand = 12;

uuids.title: Random keys, ordered keys
uuids.hint: Sort these by value. A UUIDv7 sorts in creation order, and a UUIDv4 doesn't.
uuids.setup:
CREATE TABLE ids (n int, v4 uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(), v7 uuid DEFAULT uuidv7());
INSERT INTO ids (n) SELECT generate_series(1, 10);
uuids.query: SELECT n, v7 FROM ids ORDER BY v7;

presets.label: Sort the v4 column
presets.sql: SELECT n, v4 FROM ids ORDER BY v4;

presets.label: When was it made?
presets.sql: SELECT n, uuid_extract_timestamp(v7) AS made_at FROM ids ORDER BY v7 LIMIT 3;
